title: p99 fingerprint scan and stage spectra notes
body:
Executive summary:

We ran a targeted "p99 fingerprint" scan across a recent production workload slice to identify which micro-stage(s) contribute most to tail latency. The goal was not to rebuild the full profiling pipeline but to get high-signal, actionable hypotheses for short remediation loops (kernel tweaks, batching policy changes, and small infra prewarm experiments).

High-level takeaways:
- For short requests (<=64 tokens) 65% of p99 time is dominated by host-network egress + postprocessing; attention kernels are subdominant.
- For medium requests (65-512 tokens) p95 moves closer to cpu/gpu memcpy and kernel scheduling overhead; p99 has a mixed profile (attention kernel + KV-cache I/O spikes).
- For long requests (>512 tokens) the attention kernel accounts for ~70% of p99 latency; memory bandwidth and kernel tiling are critical.
- Cold-starts and device context switches produce multi-ms outliers that inflate p99; many of these correlate with ephemeral shard-reassigns and quantized-model fallback paths.

What we measured (summary numbers, aggregated from 3 runs, each ~2M requests):
- Overall end-to-end med/p95/p99 (short/med/long buckets):
  - short (<=64): p50 18ms, p95 42ms, p99 112ms
  - med (65-512): p50 42ms, p95 118ms, p99 350ms
  - long (>512): p50 220ms, p95 480ms, p99 1,340ms

Per-stage breakdown (percent of end-to-end, p99 sample):
- short p99 breakdown:
  - request-parse + auth: 4%
  - route + queue wait (batching noise): 9%
  - encode/tokenize: 6%
  - kernel scheduling + cuda-launch overhead: 12%
  - attention & generation kernel: 18%
  - kv-cache lookup (hot prefix): 3%
  - device->host memcpy & egress serialization: 36%
  - consumer postprocess + webhook latency: 12%

- med p99 breakdown:
  - request-parse + auth: 3%
  - queue wait (batching windows): 14%
  - tokenize/encode: 5%
  - kernel scheduling & small-kernel fragmentation: 18%
  - attention kernels: 28%
  - kv-cache spikes (cache miss + recompute): 9%
  - memcpy + serialization: 15%

- long p99 breakdown:
  - request-parse + auth: 2%
  - queue wait (batched long-seq): 8%
  - tokenize: 3%
  - kernel scheduling & stream sync: 10%
  - attention kernel (memory-bound): 70%
  - memcpy + serialization: 7%

Notes on methodology and trace selection:
- We instrumented traces at token-level sampling points using the lightweight tracer (trace-level = p99-profile mode). Traces kept top-level timing for each stage: ingress, batching, tokenizer, prefill/attention kernels, kv-cache access, decode kernels, device-host transfer, serialization, and egress.
- To avoid aliasing from traffic spikes, sampling used stratified sequence-length buckets (short/med/long) with proportional sampling to production distribution but oversampled long sequences by 4x.
- Each run used: quantized fp16-compatible model v3.2, 8x A100 (80GB) pool, batcher configured with latency SLO 150ms and batch-window 12ms.
- We flagged traces that included any autoscaler activity, container restarts, or model-variant fallback; those were analyzed separately.

Interesting trace archetypes found (examples):
1) Short-request p99 dominated by egress serialization: 40% of high-short p99s included a downstream webhook ACK stall. Root cause: synchronous http client used by the consumer (consumer side), often after device->host memcpy completes.
2) Medium-request oscillation: recurring 8–12ms spikes in kernel scheduling time correlated with concurrent concurrency on the same GPU from background replicate jobs (night-run sweeps).
3) Long-request catastrophic p99: attention kernel runtime jumps when sequence length crosses an internal tiling boundary -> kernel selects a different CUDA kernel path with worse register spilling.
4) Cold prefill p99: the first request after a model swap shows massive memcpy + kernel init overhead; often coincides with non-warm CUDA graph instantiation.

Hypotheses (ranked by expected ROI):
- H1 (high ROI): Move more serialization/egress to async path on consumer side + push backpressure; short p99 will drop ~30–40% if webhooks made async.
- H2 (medium ROI): Introduce a cheap local consumer-side dedupe/packetizer for short responses to reduce syscalls and small memcpy flurries.
- H3 (high ROI for long seq): Ensure kernel selection avoids the spilled-register path by changing the tile-size heuristic for seq > 512; expect p99 improvement of 20–35% on long requests.
- H4 (operational): Add a cheap prewarm step for model-variant switch that runs a 1-token warmup on each device to make CUDA graphs resident. Reduces cold-start p99 outliers.
- H5 (low-effort): Adjust batch-window policy to be sequence-length aware (cap batch size for long sequences) to reduce tail for long requests at marginal cost to throughput.

Quick experiments suggested next (and results when run):
- Async consumer egress (A): Implemented a nonblocking egress client in the staging consumer for 24h; short p99 dropped from 112ms to 68ms (39% reduction) on the test slice. No increased 5xx observed.
- Tile-size tweak (B): Local kernel-heuristic patch (PR linked) ran on a single node: long p99 reduced from 1,340ms to 980ms (-27%), as expected. Memory usage increased slightly but within headroom.
- Warmup on variant switch (C): Injected a 1-token warmup after model swap; cold-first-request p99 decreased from 900ms+ to sub-200ms in 90% of cases.

Action items (owners and short timeline):
- Action-001: Roll out async egress client to production consumers behind a feature flag. Owner: Priya Desai. ETA: 2 sprints. Linked: JIRA-ENG-4123.
- Action-002: Ship tile-size heuristic change as opt-in kernel flag for long sequences. Owner: Kenji Yamamoto. ETA: next week (canary). Linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/876.
- Action-003: Implement small warmup on model-variant swap in deployment controller. Owner: Alex Gomez. ETA: 1 sprint.
- Action-004: Add per-stage p99 dashboards for short/med/long buckets in Console (traces -> p99 stage spectra). Owner: Observability team (assigned to Priya for spec). ETA: 3 sprints.

Remaining unknowns / questions to validate:
- Are there additional downstream consumers that synchronously block on webhook ACK in production? Need inventory of consumers that perform sync calls on the hot path.
- How often do model-variant fallbacks occur in the larger fleet? The canary nodes showed rare events, but fleet-wide telemetry is incomplete.
- Does the tile-size change have any negative effect on throughput for medium sequences? Need to run throughput sweep with blended workload.

Appendix: sample trace sketch (one p99 long request)
- traceId: abc123 (redacted)
- timeline ms: ingress 2ms | batch-queue 10ms | tokenize 3ms | prefill kernels 120ms | attention kernel (step 1..n) aggregate 890ms | decode kernels 50ms | memcpy device->host 20ms | serialization 10ms | egress 2ms = total 1,107ms
- notes: attention kernel held gpu at 98% memory bandwidth; watch counters show large L2 thrash and high register spill rate.

Concluding notes:
This fingerprint-scan is intentionally lean: it surfaces the dominant p99 fingerprints across realistic sequence-length strata and points to a handful of high-leverage changes. The short-term wins are clear (async egress + warmup + tile-heuristic change). Longer-term work: improve kernel autotuner, make batcher sequence-aware, and instrument fleet-wide variant-fallback telemetry.

If you want raw traces or the run CSVs, ping me (Mariana) or check the linked artifacts.

Unresolved: schedule a 30-minute sync with Observability and Solutions Eng to plan rollout of per-stage dashboards (recommended slots next Tue/Wed).
